# Osprey (01, architect) — SPD-096

## Brief
Settle the design of a parked bucket for the board, and write it down as a design
note the engineer on this ticket will build from. You decide; you do not implement.
No code changes, no CLI changes, no `.base` changes — a document only.

## The problem

Read `ledger/tickets/SPD-096.md` for the full statement. In short: ticket status is
`queued|active|done|declined`, `queued` is a 46-deep backlog, and priority is the only
sort inside it. A ticket that is genuinely important but deliberately not-now has
nowhere to go but a priority that lies about it. On 2026-09-16 Eric parked six BadTakes
tickets by tagging them (`deferred` on BAD-040, BAD-041, BAD-042, BAD-043, BAD-048;
`waiting` on BAD-021). Nothing reads those tags, so `spud board` still opens with the
four P1 splits every session, and the `SessionStart` hook still injects them.

## The three questions, in order

1. **Tag or status.** A fifth ticket status (`deferred`) makes the state machine enforce
   parking and puts it in every rendered note and Bases view for free; it costs a
   migration, new legal transitions, and hook/render/board changes. A tag costs nothing
   structural but is enforced by nobody and must be read explicitly everywhere it
   matters. Pick one and say why, in terms of what actually goes wrong under each in six
   months. This is the expensive-if-wrong half — a fifth status is hard to walk back.
2. **What the board does by default.** Hide parked tickets behind a flag (`--all`), sort
   them last regardless of priority, or group them under their own heading. Whatever you
   choose must also hold for `spud board --brief`, which the `SessionStart` hook injects
   — that injection is the surface that actually nags, and SPD-048 (queued) already wants
   that context smaller. Say what `spud board`, `spud board --brief` and the hook
   injection each print, concretely, with a sketch of the output.
3. **Whether `waiting` differs from `deferred`.** Waiting on an external event (BAD-021
   waits on App Store approval) resolves on its own and is worth resurfacing when it
   might have resolved; deferred is a choice and is not. Decide whether that difference
   earns a second mechanism, one mechanism with a reason field, or nothing at all.

## Constraints you must respect

- One writer: `bin/spud` is the only program that writes the ledger database. Whatever
  you choose, a parked ticket must be set and unset by a `spud` command, never by hand.
- If you choose a status: name the migration (`0003_*`), the exact new CHECK constraint,
  every legal transition into and out of it, what `ticket move` accepts, what the
  `BOARD` ordering SQL in `bin/spudlib/state/schema.py:193` becomes, and what every
  place that enumerates statuses must learn (grep for them; do not guess the list).
- If you choose a tag: name exactly which code reads the tag, how it is set and cleared,
  and what stops it from silently rotting the way it just did.
- Obsidian: `ledger/Board.base` needs a view for parked tickets and its Board and
  By project views need to exclude them. Specify the filter expressions in Bases syntax,
  matching the style already in the file. Spud makes that edit himself — write the exact
  YAML he should paste, do not edit the file.
- Rendered ticket notes carry the status in frontmatter. Say what a parked ticket's
  frontmatter looks like and whether any existing note's bytes change.
- `spud board --help` must document how to see parked tickets. Draft that line.
- The six tickets above must read correctly under your mechanism. Say what each becomes.

## Deliverable

`docs/design/2026-09-16-parked-tickets.md` — a design note, not an essay. Structure it as:
the decision (one paragraph, up front), why, what the board prints (with output sketches),
the implementation checklist the engineer follows in order, and the risks you accept.
It must be specific enough that an engineer who has not read this brief can build from it
without a second design pass. Name real files and real line numbers.
